newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rebound, bonds and the dollar rally.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rebound, bonds and the dollar rally.

text.p: Stocks bounced back on Monday as investors snapped up bargains after last week's huge sell-off.
Bonds and the dollar also rallied, while cattle prices tumbled.
Blue-chip stocks rebounded strongly after posting their second-biggest point loss ever on Friday.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 108.70 points, or 1.4 percent, to 7,803.36, regaining almost half of Friday's 247-point decline, which was the biggest percentage drop in nearly six years.

Despite the recovery in the 30-share Dow, many investors remained unsure of the market's short-term direction. In broader trading, declining issues led advances by a narrow margin, 1,461 to 1,393, on an active volume of 514 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said blue-chip issues raced higher as investors sought bargains in well-known corporate names after Friday's rout.
"This was a very good first step" after Friday's losses, said Brad Weekes, managing director of equity trading at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Inc.
Despite Friday's drop, money managers saw little sign that assets were being reallocated in investment portfolios.

"We have not seen any and we don't intend to make any," said James Walline, vice president, equities and mutual funds at Lutheran Brotherhood. "The market has stabilized this morning and frankly we don't see any reason to reallocate."
A strong bond market, a stable dollar and the underlying belief that the economy was still in good shape helped fuel Monday's rebound, Weekes said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.52 percent from 6.55 percent on Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The dollar rose against the Japanese yen and the German mark, buoyed by the recovery on Wall Street and remarks from a member of Germany's central bank that cast doubt on prospects for higher German interest rates.
The dollar edged up to 1.8340 marks from 1.8190 late on Friday. It also rose to 118.00 yen from 117.42 on Friday.
Wall Street was also bracing for Tuesday's Federal Reserve policy-makers' meeting, though the betting was the central bank would hold interest rates steady.

In commodities, cattle prices fell sharply following a government report predicting a surprisingly big cattle herd. Concerns that consumer demand for beef may be hurt by a food safety scare also hit prices.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, live cattle for October delivery fell the allowable daily trading limit of 1.50 cents a pound to close at 68.70 cents.

The Agriculture Department on Friday said Hudson Foods Inc. of Rogers, Ark., had recalled 1.2 million pounds of ground beef on suspicion of contamination by E.coli bacteria. Health officials blamed the bacterium for 16 cases of illness in Colorado in July.
Overseas, Britain's FTSE 100 fell 30.8 points, or 0.63 percent, to 4,835.0. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 19,041.10, down 284.93 points, or 1.47 percent.
